title: Nonna's Focaccia, Finally Cracked (48-Hour Cold Proof)
creator: Teo Marchetti
description:
I've been chasing my nonna's focaccia for three years. This is the one.

Recipe (grams): 500 bread flour, 400 water, 10 salt, 4 instant yeast, a frankly irresponsible amount of olive oil.

This video is sponsored by Kestrel Knives: 15% off your first knife with code TEO15 at https://kestrelknives.com/teo

Instagram: @teocooks

sentences.t: Okay, the focaccia is out of the oven, and I need you to just listen to this crust for a second.
Hear that?
That crackle is the entire reason we did a forty-eight hour cold proof in the fridge.
I'm going to cut into it while it's still way too hot, which, yes, I know, everyone says let it rest.
I never let it rest.
Life is short, and focaccia is best when it burns your fingers a little bit.
Look at that crumb, look at those holes, that's what all the folding on day one was for.
So let's do a quick recap of what actually mattered here, because I threw a lot at you.
Number one, the hydration.
We went to about eighty percent, which feels like soup when you first mix it, and that's fine, trust the soup.
Number two, the oil.
Don't be shy with it, you want the bottom of that pan basically shallow frying the dough.
My nonna used so much oil that my grandfather used to joke she was building a boat, not baking bread.
Number three, the dimpling.
Push your fingers all the way down until you feel the pan, and don't be gentle, this is the one time you get to be aggressive with dough.
And number four, the cold proof, which is the step people skip and then wonder why their focaccia tastes like a kitchen sponge.
Time is the ingredient you can't buy, as my nonna would say, usually while doing something I wasn't allowed to help with.
Okay, taste test.
Mmm.
Oh, that's salty in the best possible way.
The rosemary went crispy on top, the cherry tomatoes kind of collapsed into jam, and the bottom is basically one giant crouton.
I'm actually a little emotional, this is the closest I've ever gotten to hers.
If you make this, please tag me, I want to see your dimples, and I mean the bread ones.
And if yours comes out flat, don't panic, it's almost always old yeast or a fridge that's too cold, and I'll pin a comment about that.
Next week we're doing fresh pasta with no machine, just a rolling pin and a lot of patience.
Thank you so much for watching, seriously, this channel is just me and a very small kitchen, so every view means a lot.
